en: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method of movement;
this [method] enables one to cross over, being established upon the path of yoga consisting of the three wheels. 1.1.
That which was concealed in the Tantra, arranged both in direct and reverse order,
has been taught according to its summary (uddeśa) and likewise according to its detailed exposition (nirdeśa).
This detailed exposition of the entire procedure for the ritual conventions, by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner shall attain accomplishment. (1.3)
The factors conducive to enlightenment are established through thirty-seven applications;
they are renowned and made manifest in the world by Śrī Heruka, the supreme one of the universe. 1.4
First of all, the Lord of Yoga should generate the divine ego within the five aggregates. 1.5.

In the aggregate of form is Vairocana; in the aggregate of feeling is Vajrasūrya; in the aggregate of perception is Padmanarteśvara; in the aggregate of mental formations is Vajrarāja; in the aggregate of consciousness is Vajrasattva; but Śrī Herukavajra is the self of all the Tathāgatas. 1.6

The Vajra of Delusion is in the two eyes; the Vajra of Hatred is in the two ears; the Vajra of Envy is in the two nostrils; the Vajra of Passion is in the mouth; the Vajra of Avarice is in touch; and the Vajra of Sovereignty is in all the sense bases.

Regarding "the element of Śrī Heruka": the earth element is Pātanī; the water element is Māraṇī; the fire element is Ākarṣaṇī; the wind element is Padmanarteśvarī; and the space element is Padmajālinī. (1.8)
In this way, one should generate the sense of divine identity regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields. 1.9.
Thus ends the first chapter, the instruction on the purification of the abodes of the deities, in the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*.

Now, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening should be applied by way of their correspondence with deities. What, then, are they all? 2.1: [They are as follows: (1) the four foundations of mindfulness; (2) the four right endeavors; (3) the four bases of psychic power; (4) the five faculties; (5) the five powers; (6) the seven factors of awakening; and (7) the eightfold noble path. Among these, the four foundations of mindfulness are: (1) the foundation of mindfulness of the body; (2) the foundation of mindfulness of feelings; (3) the foundation of mindfulness of the mind; and (4) the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena. The four right endeavors are: (1) the right endeavor to prevent unarisen unwholesome states from arising; (2) the right endeavor to abandon arisen unwholesome states; (3) the right endeavor to produce unarisen wholesome states; and (4) the right endeavor to maintain and increase arisen wholesome states. The four bases of psychic power are: (1) the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire accompanied by effort; (2) the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of energy accompanied by effort; (3) the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind accompanied by effort; and (4) the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation accompanied by effort. The five faculties are: (1) the faculty of faith; (2) the faculty of energy; (3) the faculty of mindfulness; (4) the faculty of concentration; and (5) the faculty of wisdom. The five powers are: (1) the power of faith; (2) the power of energy; (3) the power of mindfulness; (4) the power of concentration; and (5) the power of wisdom. The seven factors of awakening are: (1) the factor of awakening that is mindfulness; (2) the factor of awakening that is investigation of phenomena; (3) the factor of awakening that is energy; (4) the factor of awakening that is joy; (5) the factor of awakening that is tranquility; (6) the factor of awakening that is concentration; and (7) the factor of awakening that is equanimity. The eightfold noble path is: (1) right view; (2) right intention; (3) right speech; (4) right action; (5) right livelihood; (6) right effort; (7) right mindfulness; and (8) right concentration. These are the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening. Furthermore, among these, the four foundations of mindfulness are included within the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom. The four right endeavors are included within the aggregate of morality and the aggregate of wisdom. The four bases of psychic power are included within the aggregate of concentration and the aggregate of wisdom. The five faculties and the five powers are included within the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom. The seven factors of awakening are included within the aggregate of concentration and the aggregate of wisdom. The application of mindfulness to the body; the application of mindfulness to feelings; the application of mindfulness to phenomena; and the application of mindfulness to the mind. 2.2

The basis of psychic power consisting of desire; the basis of psychic power consisting of energy; the basis of psychic power consisting of investigation; the basis of psychic power consisting of mind. || 2.3 ||
The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. 2.4
The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. || 2.5 ||

The factor of enlightenment that is concentration; the factor of enlightenment that is vigor; the factor of enlightenment that is joy; the factor of enlightenment that is pliancy; the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena; the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness; and the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity. (2.6)
Right view; right resolve; right speech; right action; right livelihood; right effort; right mindfulness; right concentration. 2.7

The production of wholesome states that have not yet arisen; the preservation of wholesome states that have already arisen; the abandonment of unwholesome states that have already arisen; and the non-arising of unwholesome states that have not yet arisen. || 2.8 ||

These are the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (bodhipākṣika-dharma), beginning with the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), the five faculties (pañcendriya), the five powers (pañcabala), the seven factors of awakening (saptabodhyaṅga), and culminating in the noble eightfold path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga). || 2.9 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, the instruction on the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, in the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*.
In this regard—I shall describe the connection of these [mudrās] with their deities, in due order and in brief. (3.1)

The application of mindfulness to the body is Ḍākinī; the application of mindfulness to feelings is Lāmā; the application of mindfulness to phenomena is Khaṇḍarohā; the application of mindfulness to the mind is Rūpiṇī. 3.2

The base of psychic power of zeal is Pracaṇḍā; the base of psychic power of energy is Caṇḍākṣī; the base of psychic power of investigation is Prabhāvatī; the base of psychic power of mind is Mahānāsā. 3.3.
The faculty of faith is Vīramatī; the faculty of energy is Kharvarī; the faculty of mindfulness is Lokeśvarī; the faculty of concentration is Drumacchāyā; and the faculty of wisdom is Airāvatī. (3.4)
The power of faith is Mahābhairavā; the power of vigor is Vāyuvegā; the power of mindfulness is Surābhakṣī; the power of concentration is Śyāmā; the power of wisdom is Subhadrā. 3.5.

Hayakarṇā is the factor of awakening that is concentration; Khagānanā is the factor of awakening that is vigor; Cakravegā is the factor of awakening that is joy; Khaṇḍarohā is the factor of awakening that is pliancy; Śauṇḍinī is the factor of awakening that is the investigation of phenomena; Cakravarmiṇī is the factor of awakening that is mindfulness; Suvīrā is the factor of awakening that is equanimity. (3.6)

Right view is Mahābalā; right intention is Cakravartinī; right speech is Mahāvīryā; right action is Kākāsyā; right livelihood is Ulūkāsyā; right effort is Śvānāsyā; right mindfulness is Śūkarāsyā; and right concentration is the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka. (3.7)

The production of unarisen wholesome states is Yamadāḍhī; the preservation of arisen wholesome states is Yamadūtī; the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states is Yamadaṃṣṭrī; and the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states is Yamamathanī. (3.8)
Thus ends the third chapter, the instruction on the purification of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment as deities, in the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme non-duality of the heroes, which is the limb and sub-limb of Śrī Heruka, abiding as all his limbs and members. 4.1

In the nails and teeth is Khaṇḍakapālī; in the hair and body hair, Mahākaṅkāla; in the skin and impurities, Kaṅkāla; in the flesh, Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrī; in the sinews, Surāvairī; in the bones, Amitābha; in the kidneys, Vajraprabha; and in the heart, Vajradeha. 4.2.

In the armpits is Aṅkurika; in the bile, Vajrajaṭila; in the lungs, Mahāvīra; in the intestines, Vajrahūṃkāra; in the small intestine, Subhadra; in the stomach, Vajrabhadra; in the excrement, Mahābhairava; and at the hairline, Virūpākṣa. 4.3.
In phlegm is Mahābala; in pus, Ratnavajra; in blood, Hayagrīva; in sweat, Ākāśagarbha; in fat, Śrīheruka; in tears, Padmanarteśvara; in saliva, Vairocana; and in nasal mucus, Vajrasattva. 4.4
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the instruction on the purification of the limbs of the heroes, in the Yoginīsaṃcāra.
Now I shall also describe another [method] which accomplishes all attainments;
by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner shall obtain success. (5.1)
The inner [mandala] as it should be known, and the supreme outer mandala; how the ritual placement (nyāsa) should be applied—the compendium of the essence of all. 5.2
Having understood that the nature of the support and the supported is established as Vairambha and so forth, this is indeed the procedure according to the sequence of the Guru’s stages. 5.3.
In the center of that lotus, whose filaments are the mountain peaks and whose petals are delicate and variegated, stands the Hero, the accomplisher of all desires and goals.
One should place Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī in the directions of the lotus, as they are the accomplishers of all siddhis. (5.5)
They have two arms and one face, or they appear in various playful forms;
in the intermediate directions, however, there are four [deities], each holding five full skull-cups.
The [deities] beginning with Pukārā, established in their respective locations,
should always be brought [within] and worshipped by the knower of yoga while situated within the center of the wheel.

*Pu*: at Pullīramalaya, Khaṇḍakapālin and Pracandā; *Jā*: at Jālandhara, Mahākaṅkāla and Caṇḍākṣī; *O*: at Oḍḍiyāna, Kaṅkāla and Prabhāvatī; *A*: at Arbuda, Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrin and Mahānāsā. These are the *pīṭhas*. 5.8.

*Go* is Surāvairī and Vīramatī at Godāvarī; *Rā* is Amitābha and Kharvarī at Rāmeśvara; *De* is Vajraprabha and Laṅkeśvarī at Devīkoṭa; *Mā* is Vajradeha and Drumacchāyā at Mālava. These are the secondary seats (*upapīṭhas*). These are the Sky-farers (*khecaryas*) of the Mind Wheel (*cittacakra*). 5.9.
*Kā* is Aṅkurikā and Airāvatī in Kāmarūpa; *o* is Vajrajaṭila and Mahābhairavī in Oḍra. [In the] field. 5.10.
*Tri* refers to Mahābhairava and Vāyuvegā in Triśakuni; *ko* refers to Vajrahūṃkāra and Surābhakṣī in Kosala. [These are] in the secondary fields (*upakṣetra*). 5.11.
Ka is Subhadra in Kaliṅga, with Śyāmādevī; La is Vajrabhadra in Lampāka, with Subhadrā. These are the two Chandohas. 5.12.

*Kā* is Mahābhairava at Kāñcī, [accompanied by] Hayakarṇā; *hi* is Virūpākṣa at Himālaya, [accompanied by] Khagānanā. These are the two Upacchandohas. They are the Earth-walkers (*bhūcarīs*) of the Wheel of Speech (*vākcakra*). 5.13.
*Pre* refers to Mahābala and Cakravegā in the city of the pretas; *gṛ* refers to Ratnavajra and Khaṇḍarohā in the deity of the house. These are the meeting places (*melāpaka*). 5.14.
*Sau* refers to Hayagrīva and Śauṇḍinī in Saurāṣṭra; *su* refers to Ākāśagarbha and Cakravarmiṇī in Suvarṇadvīpa. These are the secondary meeting places (*upamelāpaka*). 5.15.
*Na* is Śrī Heruka and Suvīrā in the city; *si* is Padmanarteśvara and Mahābalā in the land of Sindhu. These two are the cremation grounds. (5.16)

*Ma* is Vairocana and Cakravartinī in the land of Maru; *ku* is Vajrasattva and Mahāvīryā in Kulūtā. These two are the secondary cremation grounds (*upaśmaśāna*). They are the deities who move through the underworld (*pātālacāriṇī*) of the Body Wheel. 5.17.
Kākāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, Śvānāsyā, and Śūkarāsyā are at the mouth. 5.18.
Yamadāḍhī, Yamadūtī, Yamadaṃṣṭrī, and Yamamathanī [are to be visualized] when facing away. || 5.19 ||
Thus, having relied upon both the external and the internal, up to the sphere of cessation.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Instruction on the Grounds for the Arrangement of Deities, in the Yoginīsaṃcāra.
Now, regarding the group of mudrās characterized by the signs of universal sovereignty and so forth,
their respective colors, arms, and postures are determined in the secret tantras.
The Great King Śrī Heruka, the crusher of all that is evil, embraces with his two hands and wears an elephant hide on both. || 6.2 ||
The battle-axe, trident, and cleaver are raised in the right hands; the skull-topped staff, skull-cup, blood-filled noose, and severed head are likewise raised. (6.3)
That which is known as *avasavya*, adorned with twenty-four [beads], should be understood as fifty; however, the sacrificial *muṇḍamālā* consists of one hundred and fifty.
Before the Blessed Lady, one should place [an image] with a single face, greatly radiant,
holding an embrace, a skull-cup, and the blood of wicked Māras.
In the south, however, one should always hold the Tarjikā, the wicked knife;
it is red in color, possessed of great flames, and has a girdle adorned with fragments.
With disheveled hair, her body possessing three eyes, and terrifying with her formidable fangs,
she encircles both shanks with her feet, forming a pair of joined palms.
The four [deities], such as the Ḍākinī and others, hold a khaṭvāṅga, a skull-cup, and a knife; they possess the five mudrās on their bodies and are adorned with loose, flowing hair. (6.8)
Adorned with the twenty-four heroes and the five mudrās and so forth, he has either two arms and one face, or [is adorned with] a crown of matted hair and a silk ribbon. (6.9)
Embracing the Vajra-bell through the passion of great desire, the twenty-four yoginīs are resplendent with their hair loosened. (6.10)
The crest-jewel of the four mudrās, three-eyed, adorned with a girdle, embracing the yogic vessel, and holding a threatening gesture and a flaying knife against the wicked. 6.11.
Śrī Heruka and all the others are established in the ālīḍha posture;
they are adorned with a necklace, a breast-ornament, earrings, and a crest-jewel. (6.12)
The sacred thread and the ash are proclaimed as the six mudrās;
purified by the six perfections, they are adorned with these six mudrās. (6.13)

The three syllables, distinguished by body, speech, and mind, are in essence one's own nature; one who desires accomplishment should meditate on the self as that very nature—what need is there for anything else? (6.14)
Even with a thousand mouths,
one could not describe the full extent of the virtues of the practitioner of that merit which arises from it.
The four [goddesses] beginning with Kākāsyā are all stationed at the gates;
treading upon a corpse with their feet, they stand in the ālīḍha posture. (6.16)
Having likewise meditated upon Yamadāḍhī, one should place her in the four corners;
similarly, having stepped upon them with the foot, there are indeed two beautiful forms.
Just as the ḍākinīs arise through the divisions beginning with Kākāsyā, so too is the sequence of the rules for the differentiation of colors for the entire wheel. 6.18.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*, concerning the instruction on one's own insignia, face, arms, color, and weapons.
Now I shall declare the determination of the two armors found in the secret tantras,
by the knowledge of which the practitioner shall indeed swiftly attain accomplishment.
Oṃ ha namaḥ hi svāhā huṃ vauṣaṭ heṃ hūṃ hūṃ ho phaṭ haṃ;
these are applied to the heart, head, crest-lock, shoulders, eyes, and weapon. (7.2)
The first is Vajrasattva, the second is established as Vairocana;
the third is Padmanarteśvara, the King, and the fourth is called Śrī Heruka. (7.3)
The fifth is Vajrasūrya, and the sixth is known as Paramāśva;
he is well-protected by these six armors.
Oṃ vaṃ ham oṃ hrīṃ oṃ hreṃ hīṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ham.
[One should assign these] to the navel, the heart, as well as the mouth, the head, the crest-lock, and the weapon-mantra. (7.5)
The first is Vajravārāhī, the second is known as Yāminī;
the third is Mohanī, and the fourth is established as Saṃcāriṇī.
The fifth is known as Saṃtrāsinī, and the sixth is considered to be Caṇḍikā;
with these six, the armor of Vajravārāhī, the non-dual yoginī of heroes, is complete.
Thus ends the seventh [chapter], the instruction on the two armors, in the Yoginīsaṃcāra.
Then—
the yogi, having identified himself with the two armors, should quickly enter the wheel of commitment (samayacakra) by means of the mudrā-mantra and visualize the wheel of knowledge (jñānacakra). 8.1
With his feet treading [the ground] and his gaze directed upward, by means of the sound of the syllable *pheṃ* from his head,
he should summon the heroes and yoginīs residing in the world-systems of the ten directions;
he should impel them with the mantra and invoke them at that very moment.
Having indeed formed the foremost knot and firmly applied the middle needle as the vajra of the thumb,
one should place it upon the region of the forehead between the eyebrows.
And one should cause it to revolve by means of the whirlpool-like rotation. || 8.3 ||
The mantra-practitioner should empower the Yoginī and the Hero by joining them with the syllable *dyā* at the tip of the nose,
and having placed the syllable *vyā* upon the knob of the excellent *liṅga*.
Together with the assembly of mantras in the mouth and other [limbs]. || 8.4 ||
One should empower the Yoginī Buddhadākinī at the navel and the heart;
and the non-dual Vīra-Yoginīvīra at the tongue and the two *avadhūtīs*. (8.5)
Ānanda is the first hero, while Paramānanda belongs to the Yoginī;
Suratānanda is indeed the whole, for he knows all the means for that bliss.
He may become heaven, the mortal world, and the netherworld (pātāla) as a single form in an instant;
this is declared to be the meditation on "I-ness" (ahammaya), while the ritual procedure for withdrawal (saṃhāra) is traditionally taught.
The ḍākinīs experience that bliss as it revolves with the left and right hands.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the instruction on the attraction and withdrawal of the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*), in the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*.
Then:
"The emanation body (nairmāṇika) is to be known; now hear about the enjoyment body (saṃbhoga) according to desire.
[It is] the Mahāyāna, the Mahāmudrā, and likewise the bestowers of the siddhis of the Yoginīs. (9.1)
There is nothing superior to Mahāmudrā; it is the most excellent among all yogas.
It is the glorious Heruka, the Great King, the Lord of all lords of yoga. 9.2
Extracted from the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, it is equal to space, free from defects, the eternal state, and identical with the wisdom of the Omniscient One. (9.3)
Śrī Heruka is the supreme hero, the confluence of all perceptions;
through the drinking of soma, there arises accomplishment, the eternal and supreme state. 9.4
Having joined the syllables beginning with *pu* and so forth, which are established in their respective locations, one should assign the twenty-four syllables as the very self of Śrī Heruka. (9.5)
But the enjoyment body (sāṃbhogika) should be known as established in the great yoga; it should briefly make known the activity for one who is intent upon the ultimate cognition. 9.6
Now, O practitioner, listen as the cessation is explained according to what was indicated:
the syllable Śrī is non-dual knowledge, and *ha* is the emptiness of causes and so forth. (9.7)
The syllable *ru* is devoid of elaboration; *ka* does not abide anywhere.
These are empty by their very nature, all-pervading, and unstruck. (9.8)
Having meditated in brief, one attains the desired accomplishment through the visualization of the three bodies: the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation bodies. (9.9)
But the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment will certainly be found there. 9.10
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Instruction on Engagement, in the Yoginīsaṃcāra.
And therefore:
"One who is weary from meditative cultivation should especially withdraw from the form of conduct;
one must not effect the separation of yoga from these practitioners of conduct. (10.1)

Having meditated upon the detailed ritual procedure as previously explained in its proper manner, one should bestow [the offerings] during rites performed according to one's own will; specifically, one should offer the *bali*.
On the tenth day of the dark fortnight, and likewise on that same day of the bright fortnight,
one should perform [the rite] while standing with feet planted and eyes gazing upward, [visualizing] the emergence of the *phetkāra* from the crown of the head.
The Vajra goddesses should be swiftly propitiated with effort through liquor and even meats,
by means of the previously mentioned applications of mudrās, mantras, and yogas.
Having protected [it], one should protect [the disciple] according to the prescribed rule. || 10.4 ||
Oṃ āralli hoḥ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! O Vajraḍākinī, you are the samaya; behold, hoḥ! 10.5
Having thus recited it three, four, or five times, the ritual substances and so forth are properly established;
they are consecrated by the Hero and Yoginī with the vajra-añjali gesture opened upwards. 10.6

Oṃ kha 2 khāhi 2! May all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, apasmāras, ḍākinīs, and so forth, accept this bali-offering! Protect the samaya! Grant me all accomplishments! Eat and drink as you please; do not transgress! Be my helpers in every way for the increase of true happiness! Huṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā! || 10.7 ||
The cremation ground and other such places are adorned for the mantra of Vīracakra and the rest;
the yogin, facing south, performs worship in the upward position. 10.8.
One should give according to one's own capacity, as indicated by the proper sequence;
having worshipped with devotion on the tenth day, beginning with the month of Puṣya, oneself.
One should give away one's entire being, which is the gathering of all perceptions;
and one should consume the *caru* offering, consecrated as the remainder from two vessels.
For such a person, prosperity comes into their hands and cannot be thwarted by anyone. (10.10)
When they are worshipped by a devoted person who has attained delight in Śrī Heruka,
they become satisfied in mind and grant boons.
For those [jewels] are held in their hands upon the earth. || 10.11 ||
At night, having loosened his topknot and being naked, the observer of the vow should offer the bali;
with himself as the essence of the yoga of Śrī Heruka, by that the Mothers are satisfied. 10.12.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, the instruction on the offering of oblations, worship, the duties of the tenth day, and protection, in the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*.
Then—the six perfections and so forth, as well as the thirty-six aspects of enlightenment;
the seats and so forth belonging to the ten stages, which consist of the supreme lifespan and the deities. (11.1)
For by whatever state the minds of men are joined, they attain the nature of that very thing, just as a crystal assumes the form of everything [it reflects]. 11.2
Thus, in whatever manner it is conceived— whether in a state of fear or fearlessness,
or merely as an object of meditative reflection— it accomplishes all ritual actions.
In this very life, the fruit of enjoyment and liberation is attained;
for I have proclaimed this meditation as the collection of the essence of all things. (11.4)
Nothing has been told by you that is false knowledge for the wise;
by means of which that [reality] should be known quickly, as declared in the lineage of the gurus.
Indeed, throughout thousands of millions of births, I have been impelled by wisdom;
I have generated perfect faith and am established in the method of the practice of yoga.
The knowledge of the wise is like a well for the dull-witted and the foolish;
it is like external treatises for one who mocks them, being a being whose inner nature has not yet been ripened. (11.7)
They too all do not know, being shrouded by the darkness of ignorance;
they are constantly devoted to conceit, with their sevenfold minds characterized by pride and the like.
They all likewise do not know the secret that is the domain of the Buddha—the absorption into Śrī Heruka belonging to the great-souled Ācārya. 11.9
Having quickly produced that accomplishment which provides immediate conviction,
it is practiced according to the rules prescribed by those who know the application of the ritual for the movement [of the vital energies].
Even they [attain] the entirety of the three worlds through the praise of the Omniscient One,
by seeing, touching, hearing, and remembering him.
In this very way, one is liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt.
[This applies even to] the erroneous placement of deities and the incorrect division of mantras.
This secret, which consists of the cultivation of the opposite [of ordinary perception], accomplishes all that is essential;
it is common to all tantras for those whose minds have been fully ripened.
Likewise, the commitment (samaya) of the mantras beginning with Anuyoga has been shown;
thus it is stated in the *Tathāgatāśvāsa*: "The pure body is free from affliction. (11.14)
It is obtained by practitioners of little merit through my own satisfaction. || 11.15 ||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the Exposition of Universal Purity, in the Yoginīsaṃcāra.
Then:
neither to be protected nor to be consumed,
neither the mandala-member nor the mandala itself.
In brief, there is no recitation of mantras, no austerity, and no fire-offering; [the practice] consists of the assembly of the mind. 12.1
The object of perception for the knowledge of consciousness belongs to the Guru who is intent upon teaching;
it is not for those outside the path, even by means of scripture, let alone from afar. (12.2)
But by means of skillful methods, the teacher who reveals the heroes [teaches] the yogins— those intent on service to the guru—
the characteristics, the scripture, the enumeration, and the principles.
The self whose nature is the yoga of instantaneous form, like a seal of instantaneous form, instantaneous in every respect—being instantaneous, one should utter the mantra. (12.4)
Smiling, gazing, touching with the hand, embracing, and the union of two organs— these are said in the *Tathāgatāśvāsa* to be practiced in successive order, each subsequent one being superior.
Right here, however, another worm has been pointed out, like chaff;
that alone is the life-breath of living beings, that alone is the supreme syllable.
He alone is all-pervasive, established within every body;
he alone is the knower of the Buddha’s wisdom, and he is called Śrī Heruka. 12.7
He is both male and neuter, the primordial source, and even the subtle body because he sustains it.
Whatever beings have arisen from that knowledge are established upon the earth.
And all the treatises are established upon the conclusions of the Vedas;
for without them, there is no accomplishment in this world or in the next.
It is the single, established essence of the entire doctrine of the Vedas.
May this entire world, whose nature is the five Buddhas, behold this divine and variegated drama,
for which the sixth is known by the name "Buddha."
It dances alone with manifold moods. || 12.11 ||
Furthermore, [the sequence consists of] the station and emergence, as well as the entry and accomplishment;
then the empowerment, the consecration, meditative absorption, worship, and the withdrawal. (12.12)
Now, herein lies that which is known as the ritual procedure, the non-duality of wisdom and skillful means;
from that very source have all those who effect emanation and reabsorption emerged. (12.13)
a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha ja jha ña
ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ta tha da dha na pa pha ba bha ma
ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha kṣaḥ || 12.14 ||
This, O Blessed One, is that god, the supreme consecration,
the origin of all gods, of mantras, and of the tantras themselves.
The yogi who constantly meditates upon this, always recites it, and always contemplates it—having first uttered it—shall become the non-dual Śrī Heruka. 12.16.
There, the girdle is the ornament of the Lord and the abode of all;
one should always and constantly wear this, which brings about the awakening to all dharmas. || 12.17 ||
Having meditated on the vowels and consonants (ālikāli) before him through the great yoga until he is at rest,
he should visualize a full lunar disc situated at the base of the navel.
One should contemplate the supreme syllable situated in its center;
one should visualize the form of the deity as the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind. (12.19)
For him, there is that which transcends the physical body, and even the mind does not exist in its absence;
he should contemplate the inconceivable mind, yet even that mind is not perceived.
Whether he should contemplate the inconceivable or not, he will thereafter attain the dhāraṇī.
Thus ends the twelfth [chapter], the instruction on the single word that is the reality determining all tantras, in the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*.
Now I shall further proclaim the non-dual Vīrayoginī; the place of the great yogin Śrī Heruka is the ground of the imperishable. 13.1
Pulīramalaya is on the head, and Jālandhara is on the crest-lock;
Oḍiyāna is on the left ear, and Arbuda is on the backbone. These are the *pīṭhas*.
Godāvarī is in the left ear; Rāmeśvara is between the eyebrows;
Devīkoṭa is in the two eyes; and Mālava is at the two armpits. These are the secondary seats (upapīṭhas).
Having assigned Kāmarūpa to the two armpits, Oḍra to the pair of breasts, and [Kāśmīra] to the field.
Triśakuni is in the middle of the navel, and Kosala is at the tip of the nose; these are the secondary fields (upakṣetra).
Having placed Kaliṅga in the mouth and Lampāka in the middle of the throat, these are the two *chandoha*s.
Having placed Kāñcī at the heart, one should place Himālaya at the penis; these are the two Upachandohas.
One should worship the deity residing among the pretas at the linga, and the household deity at the anus; this is the meeting place.
One should contemplate Saurāṣṭra on the two thighs and Suvarṇadvīpa on the two shanks; Upamela is at the ankles.
Having placed the city upon the fingers, and the Sindhu river upon the tops of the feet, [he should place] the cremation ground [upon the soles].
Having placed the thumb on the ring finger and the *kulūtā* (the little finger) resting upon the knee, [one should practice] in the vicinity of a cremation ground (*upaśmaśāna*).
Pu-jā-o-a-go-rā-de-mā-kā-o-tri-ko-ka-la-kā-hi-pre-gṛ-sau-su-na-si-ma-ku. (13.8)
Whether awake or asleep, standing or eating, even while engaged in sexual intercourse—wherever he may be, having fixed [his mind] there, he cannot be moved even by the three worlds. (13.9)
By him, the *Saṃvara* was extracted from the tantra named *Lakṣābhidhāna*; the reality (*tattva*) of the one-hundred-thousand-verse *Khasama-tantra* was proclaimed in its midst. (13.10)
The *piṇḍasāra* is fully explained; the *abhidhāna*, however, is situated in the arising (*udaya*).
Through brief enumeration (*uddeśa*), it is the *nirmāṇakāya*; through detailed exposition (*nirdeśa*), it is considered the *sāmbhogikakāya*.
The detailed exposition of Nirvana as a whole is indeed shown according to reality:
the three bodies known as the three wheels, characterized by the Dharma-body and the others, such as the Enjoyment-body.
The accumulation of merit for the sake of gnosis rests upon the two truths;
yet those of dull intellect, the ignorant, the mute, those of inferior wisdom, and those with wrong views [cannot grasp it]. (13.13)
Even those who mock the external scriptures are thorns on the path of the Guru;
if all of them are removed, then fame and honor will arise.
The reality of the distinction between parts and non-parts is called non-duality; the Goddess Ājñā, the adorable Sovereign, is born of the divine hero. 13.15.
Afterwards, that which effects the complete movement [of consciousness], delivers one from saṃsāra, is the Lord,
and is the manifestation of all the Vedas— that is proclaimed as the Siddhānta.
O Hero, you have explained to me that which is difficult to be understood by the followers of other Buddhas; you have followed the very path of the conventions of correct and incorrect words. (13.17)
This summary of the essential meaning has been correctly extracted from the extensive discourse on the conventions;
it is that which reveals the movement of what is not to be known, as shown by the yogi of yoga.
The exertion of those [others] is in vain, for they do not obtain that fruit;
what was spoken by the primordial being has been concealed and expressed in other ways.

Then, in the description of the movement, the practitioner who is well-composed [should perform] that which was previously taught in the Great Tantra, accomplished through the syllables of the Victor’s mantra. (13.20)
Whatever action one performs, and whatever auspicious or inauspicious thought one contemplates—all that becomes accomplished for one who has the Imperishable within. 13.21
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the Instruction on Non-duality, from the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*, concerning the determination of all rites of the *āli* and *kāli*.
Now I shall explain the secret procedure, concealed in all tantras:
the hero-yogin, seated upon the thrones of the four Buddhas, beginning with Vajra.
The Ḍākinīs and so forth are the pervasive lord of the Vajra, the Lord of Yoginīs; while the four, beginning with the Mirror-like Wisdom, arise from the yoga of non-duality within non-duality. (14.2)

Those who have reached the further shore of the six perfections should offer non-dual substances such as flowers, even a single blossom, as well as their bodies adorned with the five mudrās and other ornaments.
The hand-worship and other rites are to be known by the wise and heroic ones;
the six Yoginīs as before, and the twelve beginning with Vajrasattva. (14.4)
He who knows that the worship of the hands and so forth is difficult to obtain—the five-fifths combined, indeed mixed with Śrī Heruka—[is a true practitioner]. (14.5)
In the sacred site of Pūjanīta, a yogi who desires both worldly enjoyment and liberation may obtain his heart's desire through the worship of the hand.
Having obtained other things such as food and drink, one need not worry about them here;
through constant worship, whatever he desires is accomplished.
O Hero, this practice-vow (caryāvrata) of the Yogins, which is difficult to find on earth even for the Great Hero and the Yoginīs, is the domain of the Lord, the Master of all Yoga.
He who, having personally worshipped this [stotra], which bestows the fruits of all desires...
Thus ends the fourteenth [chapter], the instruction on the union of the four heroes, the hand-offering, and so forth, in the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*.
Now I shall explain the procedure for the conduct [caryāvidhi] for the hero and the non-dual yoginī:
first, the yogi, being composed, should diligently generate the power [śakti]. 15.1.
Thereafter, having attained the necessary capacity, the Great Hero wanders at will through the practice of vows for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. (15.2)
Seeking happiness, one who dwells in a garment made of animal skin may move about at ease;
having cast off the sacred thread, purification is established according to the tradition of Śrī Heruka. 15.3
Those who desire the fruit of liberation according to their wish should desire all the yoginīs;
that which is conceived as the hero of the root mantra, beginning with the Brahma-thread (brahmasūtra), [is to be worshipped]. 15.4.
The heart-mantra of the deity is indeed adorned with fifty [beads] in the garland;
with six [beads] for the armor, O hero—this is the mudrā that beautifies the body.
The mantra of Vajravārāhī is adorned upon her neck with a necklace;
the ḍākinīs of all the Buddhas wear garments of skin as their supreme [attire]. 15.6.
The khaṭvāṅga is the form of the deity, while the hand-drum (ḍamaru) is conceived as wisdom;
all [the other implements], such as the skull-cup and so forth, are conceived as the constituent elements of the body. 15.7
With the seven-syllable mantra, he fashioned earrings as ornaments for the ears;
and with the mantra of the six Yoginīs, he made a girdle as an ornament.
The yoginīs of the entire wheel [possess] the skull-cup for drinking the mantra;
that mantra which is Vairocanī has its crest marked with a skull.
Having reflected thus, and having always maintained celibacy while protecting oneself with the protective mantras, one should indeed recite the mantra honored by eight steps.
During the day the Blessed One is a hero, but at night he is conceived as a yoginī;
there is nothing that is not to be done, and there is always nothing that is inconceivable.
There is nothing that should not be eaten, nor anything—whether auspicious or inauspicious—that should not be spoken;
as I am in myself, so are all beings, and as they are, so am I in others. (15.12)
Having reflected thus, the hero whose self is yoga, free from all mudrās and mantras, should roam like a lion, fulfilling all hopes. 15.13
For as many as there are movements of the limbs and expansions of speech, so many are the mantras and mudrās established in the state of Śrī Heruka. (15.14)
The practice of the five colors is conceived as being of a single color;
thus, beings and so forth wander through the self, the supreme state. 15.15
There is nothing whatsoever that must not be done by one whose mind possesses non-dual knowledge;
with a single, non-conceptual mind as his very self, he may enjoy the fivefold objects of desire. 15.16
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Instruction on the Non-duality of the Mantras of the Conduct Vow, in the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*.
In this latter age, O Mañjuśrī, you will not attain accomplishment elsewhere than through the perception of the Buddha, which arises from the mudrās, the maṇḍala, and the recitation. 16.1.
Those who are tormented by hunger and thirst do not attain success or happiness;
rather, the yogin must rely on effort and the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃtattva) while maintaining his resolve.
Just as the knower of Śrī Heruka wanders according to his desire, he beholds the Yoginī in an instant with his eyes and ears of far-reaching hearing. (16.3)
Having understood these phenomena in this way, those of great wisdom, who fulfill all aspirations, practice the excellent vow of non-dual knowledge. (16.4)
If one considers this Dharma to be free from the vowels and consonants, his labor is in vain; he shall certainly not obtain its fruit. (16.5)
Through the divisions of the Sūtras, Kriyā, and Abhicāra, as well as Yoga, Guhya, and so forth,
it has been proclaimed for the purpose of awakening and as a cause for all the world.

But one who knows the reality of the nature of phenomena understands that the two accumulations proceed as previously described, yet are non-dual; for him, there is considered to be nothing but nirvāṇa.
I have previously stated that everything is based upon the two truths; it is held that a yogi, with his whole being, should take delight in meditative cultivation.
Having taken all conceptual proliferation as its object, that which is non-proliferated within proliferation—the secret Nirvāṇa found in all tantras—has been revealed. (16.9)
For this reason, the yogi, having relied upon the two truths and having dispelled all conceptual thought, partakes in all enjoyments and pleasures. (16.10)
The great yogi shall wander within the commitment of the Cakrasaṃvara;
for this yoginī, there is a sign consisting of a form-convention and a secret code.
The Cakrayoginī resides indeed in villages such as Gṛhapañca;
when she is propitiated, everything thereafter proceeds by way of counter-clockwise rotation.
Having duly drawn the aforementioned wheel according to the rules, the practitioner, observing the vow,
should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Vīra-mantras, the Yoginīs, and so forth, as desired by his mind.
On the front leaf, the ḍākinīs are visualized in the form of donkeys;
this ritual procedure known by the name Śrīherukī is indeed effective for all rites.
Whatever action—whether spoken, unspoken, or contemplated—is performed through body, speech, and mind, all that is swiftly accomplished by one established in the state of Śrī Heruka. 16.15
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the instruction on the determination of accomplishment and the transformation into Śrī Heruka, in the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*.
Then:
The emanation of Śrī Heruka is the sixth, created by the mind;
the emanation of the Pure Dharma is shown in the form of Vārāhī. (17.1)
All [the deities] have emerged right there through the application of the churning and the churner;
the four beginning with the mirror are proclaimed as the "fourfold worship. (17.2)
Māmakī and the other beautiful goddesses reside upon the lotuses of the four ḍākinīs;
Khaṇḍakapāla and the others, twenty-four in number, reside upon the wheel as non-dual. (17.3)
It is proclaimed that for the hero who rescues beings from saṃsāra,
there are Krodhavijaya and the others at the gate, extending to the eighth [deity] in the corner.
Diligent in accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings through various disciplinary means, he should guard with great effort his secret place of rest. 17.5

But for the hero, from the Yoginīs onwards, as far as that which is manifested through supernatural powers (siddhi), once he has attained the fruit, he does not fall back into the ocean of existence among yogins. (17.6)
The *Tantrasārasamuccaya*, the means for disciplining [beings] within saṃsāra, has not had its detailed ritual procedures explained here for the sake of the ease of both teacher and disciple. (17.7)
The yogi’s mind finds rest, yet nirvāṇa is not shown;
he who practices thus is supreme, the purifier of all evils. (17.8)
In an instant, one perceives Buddhahood in this world and in the next, just as [one sees] the prior state of evil, or as being devoid of all auspicious marks. (17.9)

The yogi who meditates upon this on the earth, the domain of the Lord of all desires—whatever is secret among the gods and so forth, and whatever is auspicious among humans and so forth—[attains it]. (17.10)
That merit accrues to them by the name of Śrī Heruka, whether merely through meditation, or from recitation, study, and writing. || 17.11 ||
One attains the enjoyment of heaven or else the status of a universal monarch;
however, at the time of death for yogins, there are the heroes and yoginīs such as Śrī Heruka.
With hands busy with various flowers, bearing various banners and flags, they offered various songs and the sounding of various musical instruments. || 17.13 ||
Death is led to the state of the Sky-farer (khecarī) through the cessation of conceptual construction;
thus, O Great Hero, the Goddesses and Yoginīs are difficult to find on this earth. 17.14
Just as one who approves of talk about women and children,
and who engages in conversation and proclaims intimacy, may speak of the path but not of bondage.
Thus it has been shown for one who possesses such knowledge and practices yoga.
Now, elsewhere I shall describe the seats and so forth, the abodes of the yoginīs;
there the Śrī Heruka and other yoginīs abide as heroes in non-duality. (17.16)

Pracaṇḍā is at Pullīramalaya; Caṇḍākṣī is at Jālandhara; Prabhāvatī is at Oḍḍiyāna; Mahānāsā is at Arbuda; Vīramatī is at Godāvarī; Kharvarī is at Rāmeśvara; Laṅkeśvarī is at Devīkoṭa; Drumacchāyā is at Mālava; Airāvatī is at Kāmarūpa; Mahābhairavī is at Oḍra; Vāyuvegā is at Triśakuni; Surābhakṣī is at Kosala; Śyāmādevī is at Kaliṅga; Subhadrā is at Lampāka; Hayakarṇā is at Kāñcī; and Khagānanā is at Himālaya.

In Pretapurī she is Cakravegā; in Gṛhadevatā, Khaṇḍarohā; in Saurāṣṭra, Śauṇḍinī; in Suvarṇadvīpa, Cakravarmiṇī; in the city [of Nagara], Suvīrā; in the land of Sindhu, Mahābalā; in Marudeśa, Cakravartinī; and in Kulatā, Mahāvīryā. || 17.17 ||
In these regions, those maidens who are yoginīs of non-dual heroism should be diligently cultivated; they abide always with secret mantras.
Each individual Yoginī is surrounded by a retinue numbering ten million;
the signs, characteristics, mudrās, and so forth of the Vāma-sādhana are kept secret.
For by whatever terrible deed living beings are bound,
by that very same means, through skillful application, they are released from the bondage of existence.
Having carried him across to the further shore of saṃsāra, he becomes one who possesses knowledge according to his own will;
[he is adorned with] a necklace, a breast-ornament, armlets, earrings, and the sacred thread.
Adorned with a garland of skulls upon his neck and a girdle that jingles with a humming sound,
he is encircled by a series of world-lotuses whose filaments are the mountain peaks.
The assembly of heroes and yoginīs, numbering twenty-four in total,
having mounted the Lord of Gaurī, is embraced by him who bears the insignia of the vajra and bell.
One should meditate upon the supreme state as the Great King Śrī Heruka;
then, one should always bathe the body with fragrant water. (17.24)
One whose limbs are fragrant should adorn oneself with ashes, mudrās, and garments;
one's form should be covered with colored pigments, and one’s own dress should be changed.
For one engaged in the vow of conduct, it should be known that [the yoga] is well-established;
it is indeed bodily, vocal, as well as acquired and emotional. (17.26)

These four modes of dramatic representation (abhinaya) are indeed to be understood by one who perceives yoga; that which is called the "representational mode" (āhāryābhinaya) is known as the method of yoga. || 17.27 ||
In that regard, within the drama, the physical exertion of the body is to be understood as the great and beautiful ornament of all costumes and attire. (17.28)
That which is to be pierced, that which is to be bound, and likewise that which is suspended from the ear;
here, earrings as well as the ornaments of mothers and other relatives are to be pierced. (17.29)

The sacred thread (brahmasūtra), the armlet (aṅga), and the pearl necklace (muktā) should always be worn; one should know that the bracelet (kuṣura) and the hand ornament (hastābharaṇa) are likewise to be put on.
The cord should have one strand, while the girdle has eight;
the belt is known to have sixteen, and the waistband twenty-five.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter of the Yoginīsaṃcāra, the instruction on the dance and conduct within the locations of the seats for the purification of the principles (tattva).
